tools.name: WebSearch
tools.description:
Search the web. Returns result blocks with titles and URLs. US-only.

- The current month is (provided in the conversation below) — use this when searching for recent information.
- `allowed_domains` / `blocked_domains` filter results.
- After answering from results, end with a "Sources:" list of the URLs you used as markdown links.

allowed_domains.description: Only include search results from these domains

blocked_domains.description: Never include search results from these domains

mode.description: "standard": the normal web search: quick and cheap; right for straightforward lookups (reference facts, official pages, documentation, well-known people, places and topics) and simple follow-up lookups. "extended": a thorough, fresh search at several times the cost and latency.

tools.name: WebFetch
tools.description:
Fetches a URL, converts the page to markdown, and answers `prompt` against it using a small fast model.

- Fails on authenticated/private URLs — use an authenticated MCP tool or `gh` for those instead.
- Fails on localhost and other hostnames without a dot; for a local server, use curl via Bash.
- HTTP is upgraded to HTTPS. Cross-host redirects are returned to you rather than followed; call again with the redirect URL.
- Responses are cached for 15 minutes per URL.

url.description: The URL to fetch content from

prompt.description: The prompt to run on the fetched content

offset.description: Character position in the page text to start reading from. Use it to read on through a page too long for one call, with the value the previous result gave.

tools.name: Read
tools.description:
Reads a file from the local filesystem.

- `file_path` must be an absolute path.
- Reads up to 2000 lines by default.
- When you already know which part of the file you need, only read that part. This can be important for larger files.
- Results are returned using cat -n format, with line numbers starting at 1
- Reads images (PNG, JPG, …) and presents them visually. Reads PDFs via the `pages` parameter (e.g. "1-5", max 20 pages/request; required for PDFs over 10 pages). Reads Jupyter notebooks (.ipynb) as cells with outputs.
- Reading a directory, a missing file, or an empty file returns an error or system reminder rather than content.
- Do NOT re-read a file you just edited to verify — Edit/Write would have errored if the change failed, and the harness tracks file state for you.

file_path.description: The absolute path to the file to read

offset.description: The line number to start reading from. Only provide if the file is too large to read at once

limit.description: The number of lines to read. Only provide if the file is too large to read at once.

pages.description: Page range for PDF files (e.g., "1-5", "3", "10-20"). Only applicable to PDF files. Maximum 20 pages per request.

allow_large.description: Set to true to read a text file, or a line range of one, that is over the usual size limits, up to what still fits in your context. Only use this when you genuinely need all of it or the user asked for the whole file; otherwise read it in parts with offset and limit, or search it.

tools.name: Write
tools.description:
Writes a file to the local filesystem, overwriting if one exists.

When to use: creating a new file, or fully replacing one you've already Read. Overwriting an existing file you haven't Read will fail. For partial changes, use Edit instead.

file_path.description: The absolute path to the file to write (must be absolute, not relative)

content.description: The content to write to the file

tools.name: Edit
tools.description:
Performs exact string replacement in a file.

- You must Read the file in this conversation before editing, or the call will fail.
- `old_string` must match the file exactly, including indentation, and be unique — the edit fails otherwise. Strip the Read line prefix (line number + tab) before matching.
- `replace_all: true` replaces every occurrence instead.

file_path.description: The absolute path to the file to modify

new_string.description: The text to replace it with (must be different from old_string)

replace_all.description: Replace all occurrences of old_string (default false)

tools.name: Grep
tools.description:
Content search built on ripgrep. Prefer this over `grep`/`rg` via Bash — results integrate with the permission UI and file links.

- Full regex syntax (e.g. "log.*Error", "function\s+\w+"). Ripgrep, not grep — escape literal braces (`interface\{\}`).
- Filter with `glob` (e.g. "**/*.tsx") or `type` (e.g. "js", "py", "rust").
- `output_mode`: "content" (matching lines), "files_with_matches" (paths only, default), or "count".
- `multiline: true` for patterns that span lines.

pattern.description: The regular expression pattern to search for in file contents

path.description: File or directory to search in (rg PATH). Defaults to current working directory.

glob.description: Glob pattern to filter files (e.g. "*.js", "*.{ts,tsx}") - maps to rg --glob

output_mode.description: Output mode: "content" shows matching lines (supports -A/-B/-C context, -n line numbers, head_limit), "files_with_matches" shows file paths (supports head_limit), "count" shows match counts (supports head_limit). Defaults to "files_with_matches".

-B.description: Number of lines to show before each match (rg -B). Requires output_mode: "content", ignored otherwise.

-A.description: Number of lines to show after each match (rg -A). Requires output_mode: "content", ignored otherwise.

context.description: Number of lines to show before and after each match (rg -C). Requires output_mode: "content", ignored otherwise.

-n.description: Show line numbers in output (rg -n). Requires output_mode: "content", ignored otherwise. Defaults to true.

-o.description: Print only the matched (non-empty) parts of each matching line, one match per output line (rg -o / --only-matching). Requires output_mode: "content", ignored otherwise. Defaults to false.

type.description: File type to search (rg --type). Common types: js, py, rust, go, java, etc. More efficient than include for standard file types.

head_limit.description: Limit output to first N lines/entries, equivalent to "| head -N". Works across all output modes: content (limits output lines), files_with_matches (limits file paths), count (limits count entries). Defaults to 250 when unspecified. Pass 0 for unlimited (use sparingly — large result sets waste context).

offset.description: Skip first N lines/entries before applying head_limit, equivalent to "| tail -n +N | head -N". Works across all output modes. Defaults to 0.

multiline.description: Enable multiline mode where . matches newlines and patterns can span lines (rg -U --multiline-dotall). Default: false.

tools.name: Glob
tools.description: Fast file pattern matching. Supports glob patterns like "**/*.js" or "src/**/*.ts". Returns matching file paths sorted by modification time.

pattern.description: The glob pattern to match files against

path.description: The directory to search in. If not specified, the current working directory will be used. IMPORTANT: Omit this field to use the default directory. DO NOT enter "undefined" or "null" - simply omit it for the default behavior. Must be a valid directory path if provided.

# Proposed outline: „מאחורי הפלייליסט" (Behind the Playlist)

*Status: **approved** v1.0 · 2026-11-14 (Prompt 9): Noa approved, 20-page plan approved, diagram stays in Ch. 6. Cover details stay as marked placeholders.*
*Sources listed below are **candidates** from the Boss's own knowledge, not yet verified. The Researcher agent must open and confirm each one (or replace it) before the Writer uses it.*

## Frame

- **Format:** A4, 20 pages, XeLaTeX. Each chapter is about 2 pages.
- **Fictional listener:** **נועה** (Noa), 24, a student in Tel Aviv. She has a phone, a premium subscription to an unnamed streaming app, and strong opinions about 2000s pop. All her data is invented and labelled so.
- **Running structure of each chapter:**
  1. **Scene** (½ page): a short, humorous moment from Noa's day.
  2. **Explanation** (1–1½ pages): one mechanism, plain Hebrew, with citations.
  3. **„בקצרה"** box: 2–3 takeaways.
- **Box types** (defined once in `style.sty`):

  | Box | Purpose |
  |---|---|
  | „בקצרה" | Key takeaways (brand color) |
  | „מעבדה" | Formula or worked example (secondary color) |
  | „רגע, זה אמיתי?" | Myth vs. research, or what a company has *publicly* said (accent color) |
  | „נתונים בדיוניים" | Small grey tag on every fictional table, graph or number |

## Page plan

| Page | Section | Content | Required element |
|---|---|---|---|
| 1 | **Cover** | Title „מאחורי הפלייליסט", subtitle „איך מערכות המלצה בוחרות לנו את השיר הבא", a TikZ graphic (sound wave turning into a network), course and student details | — |
| 2 | **Abstract (תקציר)** | ~200 words on what the book explains and how. States that examples and data are fictional and models are educational simplifications. Includes a legend of the four box types. | — |
| 3 | **Table of contents** | Generated by `\tableofcontents` | — |
| 4–5 | **Ch. 1: „בוקר טוב, נועה"** (introduction) | Noa opens the app at 07:30 and the "Daily Mix" is suspiciously good. Why recommendation exists: catalogs of tens of millions of tracks, choice overload. What the book will and will not claim: we do not know any company's real algorithm. Map of the chapters. | — |
| 6–7 | **Ch. 2: „כל דילוג נספר"** (signals) | Noa skips a song after 8 seconds on the bus. Explicit vs. implicit feedback; plays, skips, repeats, saves and playlist adds as noisy signals; why a skip ≠ "I hate this". | **Python graph** (p. 7): *Noa's fictional week*, plays vs. skips by hour of day (stacked bars, about 7×24 bins). Data: `figures/data/noa_week.csv`; script: `figures/noa_week.py`. Tagged „נתונים בדיוניים". |
| 8–10 | **Ch. 3: „אנשים כמוך"** (collaborative filtering) | Noa's friends Yoni and Maya "share" her taste, and the app seems to know it. Labelled „נוסחה לימודית – לא האלגוריתם של חברה כלשהי". |
| 11–12 | **Ch. 4: „שירים כמו זה"** (content-based) | A brand-new indie song with zero plays still reaches Noa. Audio features, spectrograms and neural networks, metadata and text (playlist titles, reviews); the cold-start problem. | **Comparison table** (p. 12): collaborative vs. content-based vs. context-aware/hybrid. Rows: what it uses, strength, weakness, handles new songs?, handles new users?, a scene from Noa's day. `booktabs`, RTL. |
| 13–14 | **Ch. 5: „הפלייליסט יודע מה השעה"** (context, sessions, exploration) | Gym at 18:00 vs. studying at 23:00: the same Noa wants different music. Context (time, device, activity); sequence/session models; explore vs. exploit; bandits explained as a "slot machine" analogy, no formula. | — |

Laid out as two rows of four (snake layout), flowing right to left. P. 16 gives one short paragraph per block. |

1	# Shared brief for agents (keep short; read this instead of long prompts)
2	
3	- Book: „מאחורי הפלייליסט" (Behind the Playlist), Hebrew, ~20 pages A4, XeLaTeX. Plan: `docs/outline.md` (approved 2026-11-14).
4	- Fictional listener: **נועה** (Noa), 24, Tel Aviv student, unnamed streaming app. Her story, friends (Yoni, Maya) and all her numbers are **fictional** and must be labelled so.
5	- Honesty rules:
6	  - Keep **general methods** (from research and textbooks) apart from **documented platform claims** (what a company publicly says or publishes, attributed: "according to Spotify…").
7	  - Never present an illustrative model or formula as any company's real algorithm.
8	- Cover details (author, lecturer, course, date) are **placeholders**, e.g. `[שם המרצה – להשלמה]`. Never invent them.
9	- Hand work over through files only: `docs/agents/research-notes.md`, `book/references.bib`, `book/chapters/*.tex`, `docs/agents/review-NN.md`.
10

1	# Proposed outline: „מאחורי הפלייליסט" (Behind the Playlist)
2	
3	*Status: **approved** v1.0 · 2026-11-14 (Prompt 9): Noa approved, 20-page plan approved, diagram stays in Ch. 6. Cover details stay as marked placeholders.*
4	*Sources listed below are **candidates** from the Boss's own knowledge, not yet verified. The Researcher agent must open and confirm each one (or replace it) before the Writer uses it.*
5	
6	## Frame
7	
8	- **Format:** A4, 20 pages, XeLaTeX. Each chapter is about 2 pages.
9	- **Fictional listener:** **נועה** (Noa), 24, a student in Tel Aviv. She has a phone, a premium subscription to an unnamed streaming app, and strong opinions about 2000s pop. All her data is invented and labelled so.
10	- **Running structure of each chapter:**
11	  1. **Scene** (½ page): a short, humorous moment from Noa's day.
12	  2. **Explanation** (1–1½ pages): one mechanism, plain Hebrew, with citations.
13	  3. **„בקצרה"** box: 2–3 takeaways.
14	- **Box types** (defined once in `style.sty`):
15	
16	  | Box | Purpose |
17	  |---|---|
18	  | „בקצרה" | Key takeaways (brand color) |
19	  | „מעבדה" | Formula or worked example (secondary color) |
20	  | „רגע, זה אמיתי?" | Myth vs. research, or what a company has *publicly* said (accent color) |
21	  | „נתונים בדיוניים" | Small grey tag on every fictional table, graph or number |
22	
23	## Page plan
24	
25	| Page | Section | Content | Required element |
26	|---|---|---|---|
27	| 1 | **Cover** | Title „מאחורי הפלייליסט", subtitle „איך מערכות המלצה בוחרות לנו את השיר הבא", a TikZ graphic (sound wave turning into a network), course and student details | — |
28	| 2 | **Abstract (תקציר)** | ~200 words on what the book explains and how. States that examples and data are fictional and models are educational simplifications. Includes a legend of the four box types. | — |
29	| 3 | **Table of contents** | Generated by `\tableofcontents` | — |
30	| 4–5 | **Ch. 1: „בוקר טוב, נועה"** (introduction) | Noa opens the app at 07:30 and the "Daily Mix" is suspiciously good. Why recommendation exists: catalogs of tens of millions of tracks, choice overload. What the book will and will not claim: we do not know any company's real algorithm. Map of the chapters. | — |
31	| 6–7 | **Ch. 2: „כל דילוג נספר"** (signals) | Noa skips a song after 8 seconds on the bus. Explicit vs. implicit feedback; plays, skips, repeats, saves and playlist adds as noisy signals; why a skip ≠ "I hate this". | **Python graph** (p. 7): *Noa's fictional week*, plays vs. skips by hour of day (stacked bars, about 7×24 bins). Data: `figures/data/noa_week.csv`; script: `figures/noa_week.py`. Tagged „נתונים בדיוניים". |
32	| 8–10 | **Ch. 3: „אנשים כמוך"** (collaborative filtering) | Noa's friends Yoni and Maya "share" her taste, and the app seems to know it. User–song matrix, similar listeners, neighbourhood methods → matrix factorisation (intuition only). | **Explained formula** (pp. 9–10), in a „מעבדה" box: cosine similarity, cos θ = (a·b)/(‖a‖‖b‖). Every symbol explained in Hebrew, then a worked numerical example with a 3-song fictional matrix (Noa vs. Yoni vs. Maya), step by step, with a conclusion. Labelled „נוסחה לימודית – לא האלגוריתם של חברה כלשהי". |
33	| 11–12 | **Ch. 4: „שירים כמו זה"** (content-based) | A brand-new indie song with zero plays still reaches Noa. Audio features, spectrograms and neural networks, metadata and text (playlist titles, reviews); the cold-start problem. | **Comparison table** (p. 12): collaborative vs. content-based vs. context-aware/hybrid. Rows: what it uses, strength, weakness, handles new songs?, handles new users?, a scene from Noa's day. `booktabs`, RTL. |
34	| 13–14 | **Ch. 5: „הפלייליסט יודע מה השעה"** (context, sessions, exploration) | Gym at 18:00 vs. studying at 23:00: the same Noa wants different music. Context (time, device, activity); sequence/session models; explore vs. exploit; bandits explained as a "slot machine" analogy, no formula. | — |
35	| 15–16 | **Ch. 6: „שמונה תחנות בדרך לשיר הבא"** (the full process) | Synthesis: one pass through a generic recommendation pipeline, using Noa's evening as the running example. Presented as a common textbook/industry pattern, not any company's system. | **Eight-block TikZ diagram** (p. 15, full width): 1 איסוף אותות → 2 ניקוי ואיחוד נתונים → 3 ייצוג משתמשים ושירים → 4 יצירת מועמדים → 5 דירוג → 6 סינון וגיוון → 7 הצגת המלצות → 8 משוב ולמידה, with a return arrow 8 → 1. Laid out as two rows of four (snake layout), flowing right to left. P. 16 gives one short paragraph per block. |
36	| 17–18 | **Ch. 7: „בועה עם פסקול"** (effects and responsibility) | Noa realises she has heard the same 40 artists all year. Filter bubbles and popularity bias; diversity of listening; fairness to artists; what the research actually found (nuanced, not doom). What Noa can do: explore, hide, use "start radio" from unfamiliar songs. | — |
37	| 19 | **Ch. 8: „נועה לוחצת Play"** (epilogue) | Back to the morning scene, now understood. Six key takeaways, one per chapter. A last line of humor. | — |
38	| 20 | **Bibliography (מקורות)** | Generated with biblatex + biber, Hebrew heading, sorted by author. Target ≥ 10 sources, ≥ 4 academic. | — |
39	
40	A buffer of ±1 page is allowed (PRD: 18–24). If the text runs long, Ch. 5 and Ch. 7 shrink first.
41	
42	## Where the required elements are
43	
44	| Requirement (PRD §5.2) | Location | Built by |
45	|---|---|---|
46	| Python graph | Ch. 2, p. 7 | Boss: script + fictional CSV; Writer: caption and surrounding text |
47	| Table | Ch. 4, p. 12 (comparison) | Writer drafts; Boss styles |
48	| Formula + explanation + numerical example | Ch. 3, pp. 9–10 | Writer drafts; Boss checks the arithmetic; Reviewer verifies |
49	| Eight-block diagram (TikZ) | Ch. 6, p. 15 | Boss (uses the `\beginR…\endR` node rule from PRD §6) |
50	
51	## Candidate sources for the Researcher to verify
52	
53	| Topic | Candidate | Use |
54	|---|---|---|
55	| Implicit feedback | Hu, Koren & Volinsky (2008), *Collaborative Filtering for Implicit Feedback Datasets*, ICDM | Ch. 2 |
56	| Skips as signal | Brost et al. (2019), *The Music Streaming Sessions Dataset*, WWW | Ch. 2 |
57	| Early collaborative filtering | Resnick et al. (1994), *GroupLens*, CSCW; Goldberg et al. (1992), *Tapestry*, CACM | Ch. 3 |
58	| Matrix factorisation | Koren, Bell & Volinsky (2009), *Matrix Factorization Techniques for Recommender Systems*, IEEE Computer | Ch. 3 |
59	| Content-based audio | van den Oord, Dieleman & Schrauwen (2013), *Deep content-based music recommendation*, NeurIPS | Ch. 4 |
60	| Music recsys survey | Schedl et al. (2018), *Current challenges and visions in music recommender systems research*, IJMIR | Ch. 1, 4 |
61	| Exploration / bandits | McInerney et al. (2018), *Explore, Exploit, and Explain*, RecSys | Ch. 5 |
62	| Two-stage candidate → ranking | Covington, Adams & Sargin (2016), *Deep Neural Networks for YouTube Recommendations*, RecSys | Ch. 6 |
63	| Diversity effects | Anderson et al. (2020), *Algorithmic Effects on the Diversity of Consumption on Spotify*, WWW | Ch. 7 |
64	| Artist fairness | Mehrotra et al. (2018), *Towards a Fair Marketplace*, CIKM | Ch. 7 |
65	| Choice overload | Schwartz (2004), *The Paradox of Choice* (book) | Ch. 1 |
66	| Company statements | Spotify's official newsroom/engineering/research pages on catalog size and how recommendations work (attributed as "Spotify says...") | Ch. 1, 6 "רגע, זה אמיתי?" boxes |
67	
68	## Proposed agent flow (about 5 calls)
69	
70	1. **Researcher ×1:** verify or replace the candidates above, then write `research-notes.md` (claim → source per chapter) and `references.bib`.
71	2. **Writer ×2:** call A writes Ch. 1–4 and the abstract; call B writes Ch. 5–8.
72	3. **Boss:** style file, cover, graph, table styling, diagram, build, render.
73	4. **Reviewer ×2:** call A checks text and facts against the notes; call B checks the rendered PDF pages against PRD §8.
74	5. Fix round by the Boss and/or one extra Writer call only if the Reviewer requests changes.
75	
76	## Open questions for the user
77	
78	1. Do you approve the name „נועה" and the persona?
79	2. What course name, lecturer and submission date go on the cover?
80	3. Should the eight-block diagram stay in Ch. 6 (synthesis), or move earlier as a roadmap in Ch. 1?
81

73	### 5.3 Research and honesty rules
74	- Every factual claim about how recommender systems work, about specific companies, or about research findings cites a source in the bibliography.
75	- Sources must be verifiable: peer-reviewed papers, books, official engineering/research blogs, or reputable journalism. Each `.bib` entry has a DOI or URL where possible.
76	- Aim for at least 10 distinct sources, with at least 4 academic.
77	- Statements about Spotify or other companies are attributed to what that company has publicly said ("according to Spotify's research blog...") and never extrapolated into claims about its actual algorithm.
78	- All fictional listening data, people, and numbers are marked as fictional in the caption or the box where they appear.
79	- No invented citations. The Reviewer checks every cited source against the claim it supports.

**Title:** The Music Streaming Sessions Dataset
**Authors:** Brian Brost, Rishabh Mehrotra, Tristan Jehan
**arXiv ID:** 1901.09851 (cs.IR; also cs.HC, cs.LG)
**Venue:** Per the page's comments, this is the "Web conference 2019 version" (v2).
**Year:** First submitted 31 Dec 2018; revised 14 Oct 2020.
**DOI:** 10.48550/arXiv.1901.09851

**Abstract:** I can't quote the full abstract verbatim because quotes are limited to 125 characters. Here are key excerpts and a summary:

- The authors "release the Music Streaming Sessions Dataset (MSSD), which consists of 160 million listening sessions" (paraphrase: the dataset contains 160 million listening sessions and associated user actions).
- They also provide audio features and metadata for about 3.7 million unique tracks, which they describe as "the largest collection of such track metadata currently available to the public."
- Some sessions were collected using "a uniformly random recommendation setting," which supports counterfactual evaluation of sequential recommendations.

content.content:
**Content-based filtering:** "Uses similarity between items to recommend items similar to what the user likes."

**Collaborative filtering:** "Uses similarities between queries and items simultaneously to provide recommendations."

**Similarity measures:**

- **Cosine:** "This is simply the cosine of the angle between the two vectors." It measures the angle between the vectors, not their lengths.
- **Dot product:** "The dot product of two vectors is" the sum of the element-wise products of their components. It also equals the product of their norms times the cosine of the angle between them.
- **Euclidean distance:** "This is the usual distance in Euclidean space." A smaller distance means higher similarity.

**Title:** "How Algorithmic Confounding in Recommendation Systems Increases Homogeneity and Decreases Utility"

**Authors:** Allison J.B. Chaney, Brandon M. Stewart, Barbara E. Engelhardt

**Venue:** The page doesn't name a venue. It lists subject areas (Computers and Society, Machine Learning, Statistics/ML) and a related ACM DOI (10.1145/3240323.3240370), which points to a published version.

**Abstract excerpts:**
- On the feedback loop: the systems are often trained on data from users already exposed to recommendations, and "this creates a pernicious feedback loop."
- On confounding and homogenization: using simulations, the authors show that training on "using data confounded in this way" homogenizes user behavior.
- On utility: the homogenization occurs "without increasing utility."

**Title:** Algorithmic Effects on the Diversity of Consumption on Spotify

**Authors:** Ashton Anderson, Lucas Maystre, Rishabh Mehrotra, Ian Anderson, Mounia Lalmas

**Venue:** The Web Conference (presented)

**Year:** 2020 (published April 1, 2020)

**DOI/Link:** 10.1145/3366423.3380281 (https://dl.acm.org/doi/abs/10.1145/3366423.3380281)

**Key findings:**

- **Diversity and outcomes:** The authors report that "high consumption diversity is strongly associated with important long-term user metrics, such as conversion and retention." The page does not mention churn.
- **Algorithmic listening and diversity:** They find that "algorithmically-driven listening through recommendations is associated with reduced consumption diversity."
- **Shifts over time:** Users who grow more diverse do so by moving toward organic listening. In the authors' words, they do so "by shifting away from algorithmic consumption and increasing their organic consumption."
- **Recommendation effectiveness:** A randomized experiment indicates that "algorithmic recommendations are more effective for users with lower diversity."
- **Generalist vs. specialist:** The page does not use these terms. Its closest concept is consumption diversity, which it measures as the musical coherence of the songs a user listens to, using a song embedding.

Note that this summary is based only on the abstract and metadata on the page. The full paper was not available, so details of the methodology and results are not included.

**Title:** Explore, exploit, and explain: personalizing explainable recommendations with bandits

**Authors:** James McInerney, B. Lacker, Samantha Hansen, Karl Higley, Hugues Bouchard, Alois Gruson, Rishabh Mehrotra

**Year:** 2018

**Venue:** ACM Conference on Recommender Systems

**Abstract (excerpts):** I can't reproduce the full abstract verbatim because of the 125-character limit on quoted material, so here are the key points:

- On bandits and exploration: "The multi-armed bandit is an important framework for balancing exploration with exploitation in recommendation." Exploitation favors content with the highest predicted engagement, while "Exploration recommends content with uncertain predicted user engagement for the purpose of gathering more information."
- On prior work: the authors note that existing work has treated bandits and explanations separately.
- On their contribution: they present what they describe as the first principled method that combines bandits with explainable recommendations. The method jointly learns which explanations each user responds to, learns the best content for each user, and balances exploration with exploitation.
- On results: tests on historical logs and live traffic in a large-scale music service "show a significant improvement in user engagement."

The paper is **"The Music Streaming Sessions Dataset"** by Brian Brost, Rishabh Mehrotra, and Tristan Jehan, published at WWW 2019. The DOI is 10.1145/3308558.3313641, which is the full form of the prefix in your query. It appears on pages 2594–2600 of the proceedings, and a preprint is on arXiv as 1901.09851 ([DBLP/anthology listing](https://ir.webis.de/anthology/2019.wwwconf_conference-2019.238/)).

The dataset contains about 160 million listening sessions with user interaction data, audio features, track metadata, and playlist snapshots ([arXiv](https://arxiv.org/pdf/1901.09851)). The sessions were sampled from radio, personalized mixes, users' own collections, and popular playlists on a streaming service ([ar5iv](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/1901.09851)). A subset was collected under uniformly random recommendations, which supports counterfactual research ([arXiv](https://arxiv.org/pdf/1901.09851)). The authors were at Spotify Research, and the dataset was tied to the 2019 WSDM Cup skip-prediction challenge ([ar5iv](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/1901.09851)).

One discrepancy: a third-party listing gives the session count as roughly 150 million, while the paper and its arXiv abstract say 160 million. I'd go with 160 million from the paper itself.

The search returned the paper's abstract from several mirrors (IEEE metadata, a library catalog, and an academic PDF), and they agree.

- **Core idea:** The authors argue that implicit feedback, such as purchases, viewing habits, and browsing, can be read as both positive and negative preference signals, each with a different confidence level. These systems passively track different sorts of user behavior, such as purchase history, watching habits and browsing activity, in order to model user preferences. The authors then propose treating the data as indication of positive and negative preference associated with vastly varying confidence levels.
- **Why it's different from explicit ratings:** The paper notes that there is no direct user input about what people like or dislike, which is a key gap compared with explicit-rating research. Unlike the much more extensively researched explicit feedback, we do not have any direct input from the users regarding their preferences.
- **Contributions:** The abstract describes a factor model tailored to implicit feedback, a scalable optimization procedure, and a deployment in a television recommender. They also suggest a scalable optimization procedure, which scales linearly with the data size. It also says the algorithm compares favorably with well tuned implementations of other known methods. The authors additionally describe a way to explain recommendations produced by the factor model.

Sources note that the paper is an ICDM 2008 conference paper, pages 263–272, DOI 10.1109/ICDM.2008.22, with authors from AT&T Labs and Yahoo! Research. An R package, implicitcf, implements the algorithm. I didn't find the full abstract text beyond these excerpts, so the summary above is based on the mirrored excerpts only.

**Title:** The Unfairness of Popularity Bias in Music Recommendation: A Reproducibility Study
**Authors:** Dominik Kowald, Markus Schedl, Elisabeth Lex
**Venue:** ECIR 2020 (reproducibility track), listed as an arXiv preprint (cs.IR)
**Year:** 2019 (arXiv v1 submitted 10 Dec 2019)
**DOI:** 10.48550/arXiv.1912.04696

**On popularity bias:**
- The paper states that "recommender systems are typically biased towards popular items." In other words, less popular items tend to be underrepresented in recommendations.
- It also reports that "state-of-the-art recommendation algorithms favor popular items also in the music domain."

**On low-mainstream users:**
- The authors group LastFM users by how far their listening deviates from the most popular music in the dataset.
- They find that "the low-mainstreaminess group significantly receives the worst recommendations," meaning users whose tastes are least mainstream get the least accurate recommendations.

> Author: Researcher agent · 2026-11-14 · task: R1, verify the outline's candidate sources and hand over claim→source notes per chapter

**How to read this file**
- Format: `Claim | Source key (= key in book/references.bib) | Exact location (section/page/quote ≤25 words) | Confidence`.
- **[GENERAL METHOD]** marks findings from research or textbooks. **[PLATFORM CLAIM: X]** marks what company X publicly states about itself. Attribute these in the text ("according to Spotify…").
- Papers by Spotify researchers (anderson2020algorithmic, mehrotra2018towards, mcinerney2018explore, brost2019music) are **peer-reviewed research**. They describe experiments or datasets. They are *not* descriptions of Spotify's production algorithm. Cite them as "researchers at Spotify found/reported…", never as "Spotify's algorithm does…".
- Quotes come from abstracts or from the page text opened on 2026-11-14. Where only the abstract could be opened, the location given is "Abstract".

---

## Ch. 1: „בוקר טוב, נועה" (why recommendation exists; catalog size; choice overload)

- Spotify states that its catalog has over 100 million tracks, 8 million podcast titles and 800,000 audiobooks (the last "in select markets"). **[PLATFORM CLAIM: Spotify]** | spotify2026company | Company-info page: "over 100 million tracks"; "8 million podcast titles"; "800,000 audiobooks in select markets". The figures are undated on the page; accessed 2026-11-14 | Confidence: high (that Spotify says it). Write it as "according to Spotify, as of Nov 2026".
- Spotify states that it has 788 million users and 306 million subscribers in 184 markets. **[PLATFORM CLAIM: Spotify]** | spotify2026company | "788 million users"; "306 million subscribers"; "in 184 markets" (undated, accessed 2026-11-14) | Confidence: high (that Spotify says it)
- Research literature describes commercial music catalogs as holding tens of millions of pieces. **[GENERAL METHOD]** | schedl2018current | §2.1 "Particularities of music recommendation", Magnitude of items: "The size of common commercial music catalogs is in the range of tens of millions music pieces" | Confidence: high
- Music items are short (about 3–5 minutes), are often consumed in sequence and in the background, and may be enjoyed again when repeated. This sets music recommendation apart from recommending films or books. **[GENERAL METHOD]** | schedl2018current | §2.1: "the duration of music items usually ranges between 3 and 5 minutes"; "Music is often consumed passively, in the background." | Confidence: high
- Schwartz argues that a very large number of choices can reduce well-being (the "paradox of choice"). **[GENERAL METHOD: popular-science book]** | schwartz2004paradox | Publishers Weekly review (verified page) describes the thesis: "having all these choices actually goes so far as to erode our psychological well-being." | Confidence: medium. Present this as Schwartz's *argument*, not settled fact (see Gaps).
- Spotify publicly states that it personalizes much of what users hear and see. **[PLATFORM CLAIM: Spotify]** | spotify2026understanding | "we personalize much of what you hear and see on Spotify." (page last updated 2026-10-23) | Confidence: high
- Spotify states that people and technology work together, and that some recommendations come from editorial curation by human editors. **[PLATFORM CLAIM: Spotify]** | spotify2026understanding | "At Spotify, people and technology work together to deliver relevant recommendations."; "Some recommendations are based on editorial curation, like a pop playlist created by music editors." | Confidence: high

## Ch. 2: „כל דילוג נספר" (explicit vs. implicit feedback; skips)

- Implicit feedback means systems passively track behavior (e.g. purchase history, watching habits, browsing). Unlike explicit ratings, it gives no direct statement of what the user likes or dislikes. **[GENERAL METHOD]** | hu2008collaborative | Abstract: "Unlike the much more extensively researched explicit feedback, we do not have any direct input from the users" | Confidence: high
- Implicit data should be read as positive *and* negative preference, each held with varying confidence. This is the basis for "a skip ≠ I hate this". **[GENERAL METHOD]** | hu2008collaborative | Abstract: "positive and negative preference associated with vastly varying confidence levels" | Confidence: high
- Researchers at Spotify call skip behavior one of "two particularly important forms of implicit feedback" (the other is context switching). **[GENERAL METHOD: peer-reviewed, Spotify-authored dataset paper]** | brost2019music | §4 Dataset Analysis: "two particularly important forms of implicit feedback: user skip behavior, and their context switch behavior" | Confidence: high
- The public dataset distinguishes degrees of skipping: played "very briefly", played "briefly", "most of the track was played", or played "in its entirety". This supports explaining skips as graded, noisy signals. **[GENERAL METHOD]** | brost2019music | Table 1 column descriptions (skip_1, skip_2, skip_3, not_skipped) | Confidence: high
- Skip behavior in a session is correlated with earlier skips in the same session. **[GENERAL METHOD]** | brost2019music | §6 Conclusion: "skip behavior in a session is correlated with prior skip behavior within that session" | Confidence: high
- The dataset has about 160 million listening sessions, and part of it was collected under uniformly random recommendations. **[GENERAL METHOD]** | brost2019music | Abstract: "160 million listening sessions"; "a uniformly random recommendation setting" | Confidence: high
- Spotify states that actions such as searching, listening, skipping and saving influence how it interprets a user's taste. **[PLATFORM CLAIM: Spotify]** | spotify2026understanding | "actions such as searching, listening, skipping, or saving to Your Library influence our interpretation of your taste." | Confidence: high. Note: the page does **not** mention playlist adds, repeats or time of day as signals. Do not attribute those to Spotify.

## Ch. 3: „אנשים כמוך" (collaborative filtering; cosine; matrix factorisation)

- An early (1992, Xerox PARC) paper used the term "collaborative filtering" in its title. It describes the experimental Tapestry system. **[GENERAL METHOD: history]** | goldberg1992using | Title and bibliographic record, CACM 35(12):61–70 (Crossref). Full text not opened | Confidence: medium. Use it only for the date and name, not for detailed claims about how Tapestry worked.
- GroupLens (1994) predicts scores from other people's ratings, based on the heuristic that people who agreed in the past will probably agree again. This is the core intuition of "people like you". **[GENERAL METHOD]** | resnick1994grouplens | Abstract (authors' HTML version): "Collaborative filters help people make choices based on the opinions of other people."; "people who agreed in the past will probably agree again." | Confidence: high
- Collaborative filtering uses similarities between users (queries) and items at the same time. Content-based filtering uses similarity between items. **[GENERAL METHOD]** | google2026candidate | "Uses similarities between queries and items simultaneously to provide recommendations." (CF); "Uses similarity between items to recommend items similar to what the user likes." (content-based) | Confidence: high
- Cosine similarity is a standard similarity measure: "simply the cosine of the angle between the two vectors". Other measures are the dot product and Euclidean distance. **[GENERAL METHOD]** | google2026candidate | Section on similarity measures: "This is simply the cosine of the angle between the two vectors." | Confidence: high. The Ch. 3 formula cos θ = (a·b)/(‖a‖‖b‖) is the standard textbook definition and remains labelled educational.
- Items and users are mapped to vectors (embeddings) in a shared space. Items consumed by the same users end up close together. **[GENERAL METHOD]** | google2026candidate | "map each item and each query (or context) to an embedding vector in a common embedding space." | Confidence: high
- Matrix factorisation models (popularised by the Netflix Prize) outperform classic nearest-neighbour techniques and can incorporate implicit feedback, temporal effects and confidence levels. **[GENERAL METHOD]** | koren2009matrix | Abstract: "As the Netflix Prize competition has demonstrated, matrix factorization models are superior" […] "allowing the incorporation of additional information such as implicit feedback, temporal effects," | Confidence: high
- A factor (matrix factorisation) model can be tailored to implicit feedback. **[GENERAL METHOD]** | hu2008collaborative | Abstract: "This leads to a factor model which is especially tailored for implicit feedback recommenders." | Confidence: high

## Ch. 4: „שירים כמו זה" (content-based audio; cold start)

- Cold start is the problem that arises when a new user registers or a new item is added to the catalog. **[GENERAL METHOD]** | schedl2018current | §2.2 "Challenge 1: Cold start problem": "the cold start problem, i.e., when a new user registers to the system or a new item is added to the catalog" | Confidence: high
- Collaborative filtering suffers from cold start and works poorly for new or unpopular songs. **[GENERAL METHOD]** | vandenoord2013deep | Abstract: collaborative filtering "suffers from the cold start problem" | Confidence: high
- A model can predict a song's latent factors from its audio when usage data is not available. Deep convolutional neural networks did significantly better than a traditional approach (Million Song Dataset). **[GENERAL METHOD]** | vandenoord2013deep | Abstract: "predict the latent factors from music audio when they cannot be obtained from usage data"; "deep convolutional neural networks significantly outperforming the traditional approach" | Confidence: high
- A standard content-based approach extracts features that describe the acoustic properties of the audio signal. **[GENERAL METHOD]** | schedl2018current | §2.2, State of the art: "a standard approach is to extract a number of features that define the acoustic properties of the audio signal" | Confidence: high
- Spotify states that its systems consider content characteristics such as genre and release date. **[PLATFORM CLAIM: Spotify]** | spotify2026understanding | Systems consider "genre, release date, podcast category, and signals about whether it may be AI-generated." | Confidence: high
- For the comparison table, "content-based = item–item similarity; CF = user–item similarity" can be cited to google2026candidate (see Ch. 3). **[GENERAL METHOD]**

## Ch. 5: „הפלייליסט יודע מה השעה" (context; sessions; explore–exploit)

- Situational and contextual factors strongly influence music preference and listening behavior. **[GENERAL METHOD]** | schedl2018current | §2.1: "Situational or contextual aspects have a strong influence on music preference, consumption, and interaction behavior." | Confidence: high
- Music is most often consumed in sequence, several pieces at a time, which motivates session/sequence models. **[GENERAL METHOD]** | schedl2018current | §2.1: "music pieces are most frequently consumed sequentially, more than one at a time" | Confidence: high
- A public dataset was released to support research on session-based sequential music recommendation. **[GENERAL METHOD]** | brost2019music | Abstract (dataset intended for session-based sequential recommendation; 160 million sessions) | Confidence: high
- The multi-armed bandit is a framework for balancing exploration with exploitation. Exploitation picks content with the highest predicted engagement. Exploration recommends content whose engagement is uncertain, in order to gather information. **[GENERAL METHOD: peer-reviewed, Spotify-authored]** | mcinerney2018explore | Abstract: "The multi-armed bandit is an important framework for balancing exploration with exploitation in recommendation."; "Exploration recommends content with uncertain predicted user engagement for the purpose of gathering more information." | Confidence: high
- In that study, tests on historical logs and live traffic in a large-scale music service showed a significant improvement in engagement. **[GENERAL METHOD: research result, not a description of a production system]** | mcinerney2018explore | Abstract: "show a significant improvement in user engagement" | Confidence: high
- Spotify lists device, language and location (precise location only with opt-in) among the inputs it considers. **[PLATFORM CLAIM: Spotify]** | spotify2026understanding | "your device, your language, and your location (precise location only if you opt in)" | Confidence: high. Note: the page does **not** name time of day.

## Ch. 6: „שמונה תחנות בדרך לשיר הבא" (generic pipeline; filtering/diversification; feedback loop)

- A common pattern has three stages: candidate generation (huge corpus → much smaller subset), scoring/ranking, and re-ranking under extra constraints. **[GENERAL METHOD]** | google2026overview | "In this first stage, the system starts from a potentially huge corpus and generates a much smaller subset of candidates."; "Finally, the system must take into account additional constraints for the final ranking." | Confidence: high
- Re-ranking can remove items the user explicitly disliked, boost fresher content, and help ensure diversity, freshness and fairness. This supports block 6 „סינון וגיוון". **[GENERAL METHOD]** | google2026overview | "the system removes items that the user explicitly disliked or boosts the score of fresher content."; "Re-ranking can also help ensure diversity, freshness, and fairness." | Confidence: high
- A peer-reviewed industry paper (YouTube, 2016) splits its system into the "classic two-stage information retrieval dichotomy": a deep candidate generation model, then a separate deep ranking model. **[GENERAL METHOD; describes YouTube's 2016 published system, not any music app]** | covington2016deep | Abstract: "first, we detail a deep candidate generation model and then describe a separate deep ranking model." | Confidence: high
- Feedback loop: recommenders are often trained on data from users who already saw recommendations. This "creates a pernicious feedback loop", and in simulations it homogenises user behavior without increasing utility. **[GENERAL METHOD]** | chaney2018algorithmic | Abstract: "this creates a pernicious feedback loop"; homogenization occurs "without increasing utility" | Confidence: high. Note: simulation study.
- Spotify states that tapping "not interested", thumbs down or hide leads to fewer similar recommendations. This is a platform example of block 8 (feedback → learning). **[PLATFORM CLAIM: Spotify]** | spotify2026understanding | User controls: "fewer recommendations that are similar to it." | Confidence: high
- Spotify states that its algorithms also consider trends and the general tastes and behavior of all users. **[PLATFORM CLAIM: Spotify]** | spotify2026understanding | "Our algorithms consider trends and the general tastes and behaviors of users to improve recommendations for everyone." | Confidence: high
- Spotify states that paid "Discovery Mode" increases the likelihood that selected songs are recommended but does not guarantee it. This is optional for the "רגע, זה אמיתי?" box. **[PLATFORM CLAIM: Spotify]** | spotify2026understanding | "increases the likelihood of the selected songs being recommended, but does not guarantee it." | Confidence: high

## Ch. 7: „בועה עם פסקול" (diversity; popularity bias; artist fairness)

- In a large-scale study on Spotify, algorithm-driven listening through recommendations was associated with reduced consumption diversity. **[GENERAL METHOD: peer-reviewed, Spotify-authored observational study]** | anderson2020algorithmic | Abstract: "algorithmically-driven listening through recommendations is associated with reduced consumption diversity." | Confidence: high
- Users whose listening became more diverse did so by shifting away from algorithmic listening towards organic listening. **[GENERAL METHOD]** | anderson2020algorithmic | Abstract: "by shifting away from algorithmic consumption and increasing their organic consumption." | Confidence: high
- High consumption diversity was strongly associated with long-term user metrics (conversion and retention). This is the nuance: diversity is also good for the platform. **[GENERAL METHOD]** | anderson2020algorithmic | Abstract: "high consumption diversity is strongly associated with important long-term user metrics, such as conversion and retention." | Confidence: high
- A randomized experiment found algorithmic recommendations more effective for users with lower diversity. **[GENERAL METHOD]** | anderson2020algorithmic | Abstract: "algorithmic recommendations are more effective for users with lower diversity." | Confidence: high
- Recommender systems are typically biased towards popular items, and this holds in music too. **[GENERAL METHOD]** | kowald2020unfairness | Abstract: "recommender systems are typically biased towards popular items"; "state-of-the-art recommendation algorithms favor popular items also in the music domain." | Confidence: high
- Users with the least mainstream taste received the worst recommendations (LastFM study). **[GENERAL METHOD]** | kowald2020unfairness | Abstract: "the low-mainstreaminess group significantly receives the worst recommendations" | Confidence: high
- Music streaming is a two-sided marketplace (listeners and artists). Optimising only for listener relevance can harm fairness to artists. In counterfactual evaluation, the authors improved supplier fairness without a noticeable decline in user satisfaction. **[GENERAL METHOD: peer-reviewed, Spotify-authored]** | mehrotra2018towards | Abstract: "Blindly optimizing for consumer relevance may have a detrimental impact on supplier fairness."; "fairness of representation of suppliers (i.e. artists)" | Confidence: high
- A ranking system "may be inclined to rank songs based on their popularity". **[GENERAL METHOD]** | schedl2018current | §2.4: "a RS may be inclined to rank songs based on their popularity." | Confidence: high
- What Noa can do: Spotify documents user controls ("exclude from taste profile", hide, snooze for 30 days on Premium, "not interested"). **[PLATFORM CLAIM: Spotify]** | spotify2026understanding | "When you exclude content from your taste profile, it will have less influence on your future recommendations."; snoozed tracks "won't be suggested anywhere on Spotify for 30 days." | Confidence: high. Noa's app is unnamed, so phrase this as "for example, Spotify documents…".

- Researchers at Spotify call skip behavior one of "two particularly important forms of implicit feedback" (the other is context switching). **[GENERAL METHOD: peer-reviewed, Spotify-authored dataset paper]** | brost2019music | §4 Dataset Analysis: "two particularly important forms of implicit feedback: user skip behavior, and their context switch behavior" | Confidence: high
- The public dataset distinguishes degrees of skipping: played "very briefly", played "briefly", "most of the track was played", or played "in its entirety". This supports explaining skips as graded, noisy signals. **[GENERAL METHOD]** | brost2019music | Table 1 column descriptions (skip_1, skip_2, skip_3, not_skipped) | Confidence: high
- Skip behavior in a session is correlated with earlier skips in the same session. **[GENERAL METHOD]** | brost2019music | §6 Conclusion: "skip behavior in a session is correlated with prior skip behavior within that session" | Confidence: high
- The dataset has about 160 million listening sessions, and part of it was collected under uniformly random recommendations. **[GENERAL METHOD]** | brost2019music | Abstract: "160 million listening sessions"; "a uniformly random recommendation setting" | Confidence: high
- Spotify states that actions such as searching, listening, skipping and saving influence how it interprets a user's taste. **[PLATFORM CLAIM: Spotify]** | spotify2026understanding | "actions such as searching, listening, skipping, or saving to Your Library influence our interpretation of your taste." | Confidence: high. Note: the page does **not** mention playlist adds, repeats or time of day as signals. Do not attribute those to Spotify.

## Ch. 3: „אנשים כמוך" (collaborative filtering; cosine; matrix factorisation)

- An early (1992, Xerox PARC) paper used the term "collaborative filtering" in its title. It describes the experimental Tapestry system. **[GENERAL METHOD: history]** | goldberg1992using | Title and bibliographic record, CACM 35(12):61–70 (Crossref). Full text not opened | Confidence: medium. Use it only for the date and name, not for detailed claims about how Tapestry worked.
- GroupLens (1994) predicts scores from other people's ratings, based on the heuristic that people who agreed in the past will probably agree again. This is the core intuition of "people like you". **[GENERAL METHOD]** | resnick1994grouplens | Abstract (authors' HTML version): "Collaborative filters help people make choices based on the opinions of other people."; "people who agreed in the past will probably agree again." | Confidence: high
- Collaborative filtering uses similarities between users (queries) and items at the same time. Content-based filtering uses similarity between items. **[GENERAL METHOD]** | google2026candidate | "Uses similarities between queries and items simultaneously to provide recommendations." (CF); "Uses similarity between items to recommend items similar to what the user likes." (content-based) | Confidence: high
- Cosine similarity is a standard similarity measure: "simply the cosine of the angle between the two vectors". Other measures are the dot product and Euclidean distance. **[GENERAL METHOD]** | google2026candidate | Section on similarity measures: "This is simply the cosine of the angle between the two vectors." | Confidence: high. The Ch. 3 formula cos θ = (a·b)/(‖a‖‖b‖) is the standard textbook definition and remains labelled educational.
- Items and users are mapped to vectors (embeddings) in a shared space. Items consumed by the same users end up close together. **[GENERAL METHOD]** | google2026candidate | "map each item and each query (or context) to an embedding vector in a common embedding space." | Confidence: high
- Matrix factorisation models (popularised by the Netflix Prize) outperform classic nearest-neighbour techniques and can incorporate implicit feedback, temporal effects and confidence levels. **[GENERAL METHOD]** | koren2009matrix | Abstract: "As the Netflix Prize competition has demonstrated, matrix factorization models are superior" […] "allowing the incorporation of additional information such as implicit feedback, temporal effects," | Confidence: high
- A factor (matrix factorisation) model can be tailored to implicit feedback. **[GENERAL METHOD]** | hu2008collaborative | Abstract: "This leads to a factor model which is especially tailored for implicit feedback recommenders." | Confidence: high

## Ch. 4: „שירים כמו זה" (content-based audio; cold start)

- Cold start is the problem that arises when a new user registers or a new item is added to the catalog. **[GENERAL METHOD]** | schedl2018current | §2.2 "Challenge 1: Cold start problem": "the cold start problem, i.e., when a new user registers to the system or a new item is added to the catalog" | Confidence: high
- Collaborative filtering suffers from cold start and works poorly for new or unpopular songs. **[GENERAL METHOD]** | vandenoord2013deep | Abstract: collaborative filtering "suffers from the cold start problem" | Confidence: high
- A model can predict a song's latent factors from its audio when usage data is not available. Deep convolutional neural networks did significantly better than a traditional approach (Million Song Dataset). **[GENERAL METHOD]** | vandenoord2013deep | Abstract: "predict the latent factors from music audio when they cannot be obtained from usage data"; "deep convolutional neural networks significantly outperforming the traditional approach" | Confidence: high
- A standard content-based approach extracts features that describe the acoustic properties of the audio signal. **[GENERAL METHOD]** | schedl2018current | §2.2, State of the art: "a standard approach is to extract a number of features that define the acoustic properties of the audio signal" | Confidence: high
- Spotify states that its systems consider content characteristics such as genre and release date. **[PLATFORM CLAIM: Spotify]** | spotify2026understanding | Systems consider "genre, release date, podcast category, and signals about whether it may be AI-generated." | Confidence: high
- For the comparison table, "content-based = item–item similarity; CF = user–item similarity" can be cited to google2026candidate (see Ch. 3). **[GENERAL METHOD]**

## Ch. 5: „הפלייליסט יודע מה השעה" (context; sessions; explore–exploit)

- Situational and contextual factors strongly influence music preference and listening behavior. **[GENERAL METHOD]** | schedl2018current | §2.1: "Situational or contextual aspects have a strong influence on music preference, consumption, and interaction behavior." | Confidence: high
- Music is most often consumed in sequence, several pieces at a time, which motivates session/sequence models. **[GENERAL METHOD]** | schedl2018current | §2.1: "music pieces are most frequently consumed sequentially, more than one at a time" | Confidence: high
- A public dataset was released to support research on session-based sequential music recommendation. **[GENERAL METHOD]** | brost2019music | Abstract (dataset intended for session-based sequential recommendation; 160 million sessions) | Confidence: high

Exploration recommends content whose engagement is uncertain, in order to gather information. **[GENERAL METHOD: peer-reviewed, Spotify-authored]** | mcinerney2018explore | Abstract: "The multi-armed bandit is an important framework for balancing exploration with exploitation in recommendation."; "Exploration recommends content with uncertain predicted user engagement for the purpose of gathering more information." | Confidence: high

- A peer-reviewed industry paper (YouTube, 2016) splits its system into the "classic two-stage information retrieval dichotomy": a deep candidate generation model, then a separate deep ranking model. **[GENERAL METHOD; describes YouTube's 2016 published system, not any music app]** | covington2016deep | Abstract: "first, we detail a deep candidate generation model and then describe a separate deep ranking model." | Confidence: high
- Feedback loop: recommenders are often trained on data from users who already saw recommendations. This "creates a pernicious feedback loop", and in simulations it homogenises user behavior without increasing utility. **[GENERAL METHOD]** | chaney2018algorithmic | Abstract: "this creates a pernicious feedback loop"; homogenization occurs "without increasing utility" | Confidence: high. Note: simulation study.
- Spotify states that tapping "not interested", thumbs down or hide leads to fewer similar recommendations. This is a platform example of block 8 (feedback → learning). **[PLATFORM CLAIM: Spotify]** | spotify2026understanding | User controls: "fewer recommendations that are similar to it." | Confidence: high
- Spotify states that its algorithms also consider trends and the general tastes and behavior of all users. **[PLATFORM CLAIM: Spotify]** | spotify2026understanding | "Our algorithms consider trends and the general tastes and behaviors of users to improve recommendations for everyone." | Confidence: high
- Spotify states that paid "Discovery Mode" increases the likelihood that selected songs are recommended but does not guarantee it. This is optional for the "רגע, זה אמיתי?" box. **[PLATFORM CLAIM: Spotify]** | spotify2026understanding | "increases the likelihood of the selected songs being recommended, but does not guarantee it." | Confidence: high

## Ch. 7: „בועה עם פסקול" (diversity; popularity bias; artist fairness)

- In a large-scale study on Spotify, algorithm-driven listening through recommendations was associated with reduced consumption diversity. **[GENERAL METHOD: peer-reviewed, Spotify-authored observational study]** | anderson2020algorithmic | Abstract: "algorithmically-driven listening through recommendations is associated with reduced consumption diversity." | Confidence: high
- Users whose listening became more diverse did so by shifting away from algorithmic listening towards organic listening. **[GENERAL METHOD]** | anderson2020algorithmic | Abstract: "by shifting away from algorithmic consumption and increasing their organic consumption." | Confidence: high
- High consumption diversity was strongly associated with long-term user metrics (conversion and retention). This is the nuance: diversity is also good for the platform. **[GENERAL METHOD]** | anderson2020algorithmic | Abstract: "high consumption diversity is strongly associated with important long-term user metrics, such as conversion and retention." | Confidence: high
- A randomized experiment found algorithmic recommendations more effective for users with lower diversity. **[GENERAL METHOD]** | anderson2020algorithmic | Abstract: "algorithmic recommendations are more effective for users with lower diversity." | Confidence: high
- Recommender systems are typically biased towards popular items, and this holds in music too. **[GENERAL METHOD]** | kowald2020unfairness | Abstract: "recommender systems are typically biased towards popular items"; "state-of-the-art recommendation algorithms favor popular items also in the music domain." | Confidence: high
- Users with the least mainstream taste received the worst recommendations (LastFM study). **[GENERAL METHOD]** | kowald2020unfairness | Abstract: "the low-mainstreaminess group significantly receives the worst recommendations" | Confidence: high
- Music streaming is a two-sided marketplace (listeners and artists). Optimising only for listener relevance can harm fairness to artists. In counterfactual evaluation, the authors improved supplier fairness without a noticeable decline in user satisfaction. **[GENERAL METHOD: peer-reviewed, Spotify-authored]** | mehrotra2018towards | Abstract: "Blindly optimizing for consumer relevance may have a detrimental impact on supplier fairness."; "fairness of representation of suppliers (i.e. artists)" | Confidence: high
- A ranking system "may be inclined to rank songs based on their popularity". **[GENERAL METHOD]** | schedl2018current | §2.4: "a RS may be inclined to rank songs based on their popularity." | Confidence: high

## Ch. 8: „נועה לוחצת Play" (epilogue)

- Spotify describes the user's taste profile as the most important input for its experience. This works as the closing "why your signals matter" line. **[PLATFORM CLAIM: Spotify]** | spotify2026understanding | "We believe that your taste profile is the most important input for creating the best overall user experience." | Confidence: high
